The copies share `Person` objects, which is safe because `Person` is immutable: `edit`, `log`, `editlog`, `unlog`, `stage`, `intro`, `tag` and `untag` replace a supporter with a new `Person` rather than changing the old one. A deleted supporter's interactions are stored inside their `Person`, so undoing `delete` restores the interaction history too. Deleting a supporter also removes them as the introducer of other supporters. Since a state is the whole supporter data, one undo brings back the deleted supporter and those introductions together.
Given below is an example usage scenario and how the undo/redo mechanism behaves at each step.
Step 1. The user launches the application. The `VersionedAddressBook` is initialized with a copy of the loaded supporter data as its only state, and the `currentStatePointer` points to that state.
<puml src="diagrams/UndoRedoState0.puml" alt="UndoRedoState0" />

Step 2. The user executes `delete 2` to delete the 2nd supporter in the displayed list. After the command succeeds, `LogicManager` calls `Model#commitAddressBookIfChanged(String)` with the command text, which saves the data as it is after the deletion into the `addressBookStateList` and shifts the `currentStatePointer` to the new state.
<puml src="diagrams/UndoRedoState1.puml" alt="UndoRedoState1" />

Step 3. The user executes `log 1 nt/Called` to log an interaction with the 1st supporter. This also changes the data, so `LogicManager` commits again, causing another state to be saved into the `addressBookStateList`.
<puml src="diagrams/UndoRedoState2.puml" alt="UndoRedoState2" />
<box type="info" seamless>

**Note:** Commands do not commit themselves. `ModelManager` marks the data as changed whenever `addPerson`, `setPerson`, `deletePerson` or `setAddressBook` is called, and `Model#commitAddressBookIfChanged()` saves a state only if that mark is set and `VersionedAddressBook#hasChangesSinceLastCommit()` confirms the data really differs, then clears the mark. So every command that changes supporter data saves exactly one state, even one that changes several supporters (such as deleting an introducer). A command that fails saves none. Neither does one that changes nothing, such as `stage` with the current stage, `tag` with a tag the supporter already has, `edit` with the values the supporter already has, `editlog` with the note and date the entry already has, or `clear` on an empty list. Such a command therefore also keeps any undone states available for `redo`.
</box>

Step 4. The user decides that logging the interaction was a mistake, and executes `undo`. `UndoCommand` calls `Model#undoAddressBook()`, which shifts the `currentStatePointer` once to the left and copies that state back into the current data with `AddressBook#resetData()`.
<puml src="diagrams/UndoRedoState3.puml" alt="UndoRedoState3" />
<box type="info" seamless>

**Note:** If the `currentStatePointer` is at index 0, pointing to the state the app started with, then there is no earlier state to restore. `UndoCommand` uses `Model#canUndoAddressBook()` to check if this is the case. If so, it shows an error to the user rather than attempting to perform the undo.
</box>
The following sequence diagram shows how an undo operation goes through the `Logic` component:
<puml src="diagrams/UndoSequenceDiagram-Logic.puml" alt="UndoSequenceDiagram-Logic" />
<box type="info" seamless>
**Note:** The lifeline for `UndoCommand` should end at the destroy marker (X), but due to a limitation of PlantUML, it continues to the end of the diagram.
</box>

After restoring the data, `UndoCommand` shows all supporters, so that a restored supporter is visible even if a `find` filter was active. Its result names the undone change using the description saved with it, which `LogicManager` sets to the command as the user typed it, e.g. `Undid the last change: delete 2`. Restoring a state does not mark the data as changed, so `Model#commitAddressBookIfChanged()` saves no new state for `undo` itself. `LogicManager` then saves the restored data to the data file, as it does after every successful command.
Similarly, how an undo operation goes through the `Model` component is shown below:
<puml src="diagrams/UndoSequenceDiagram-Model.puml" alt="UndoSequenceDiagram-Model" />

The supporter shown in the detail panel is not part of the saved states. After restoring a state, `ModelManager` shows the restored version of the same supporter, found through the record lineage described in [Viewed supporter state](#viewed-supporter-state), so this works even if the supporter was renamed. If that supporter does not exist in the restored data, the detail panel is cleared.

The `redo` command does the opposite: it calls `Model#redoAddressBook()`, which shifts the `currentStatePointer` once to the right, pointing to the previously undone state, and restores the data to that state.

`undo` and `redo` take no arguments. `AddressBookParser` rejects any text after them, e.g. `undo 3`, rather than ignoring it as it does for `list`, since a user typing a count expects several changes to be undone, while only one would be.
<box type="info" seamless>

**Note:** If the `currentStatePointer` is at index `addressBookStateList.size() - 1`, pointing to the latest state, then there are no undone states to restore. `RedoCommand` uses `Model#canRedoAddressBook()` to check if this is the case. If so, it shows an error to the user rather than attempting to perform the redo.
</box>

Step 5. The user then executes `list`. Commands such as `list`, `find` and `view` do not change supporter data, so `Model#commitAddressBookIfChanged()` saves nothing for them. Thus, the `addressBookStateList` remains unchanged.
<puml src="diagrams/UndoRedoState4.puml" alt="UndoRedoState4" />

Step 6. The user executes `clear`, which changes the data, so a new state is committed. Since the `currentStatePointer` is not pointing at the end of the `addressBookStateList`, all states after the `currentStatePointer` are purged. Reason: It no longer makes sense to redo the `log 1 nt/Called` command. This is the behavior that most modern desktop applications follow.
<puml src="diagrams/UndoRedoState5.puml" alt="UndoRedoState5" />
The following activity diagram summarizes what happens when a user executes a new command:
<puml src="diagrams/CommitActivityDiagram.puml" width="250" />
The history is kept in memory only, so it starts again from the loaded data each time the app is launched.
#### Design considerations:
**Aspect: How undo & redo execute:**
- **Alternative 1 (current choice):** Saves a copy of the entire supporter data after each change.
- Pros: Easy to implement, and one mechanism works for every command, including `clear`.
- Cons: May have performance issues in terms of memory usage. With the few hundred supporters this product targets, and copies that share immutable `Person` objects, this cost is small.
- **Alternative 2:** Individual command knows how to undo/redo by itself (the Command pattern with an `undo()` method on each command).
- Pros: Will use less memory (e.g. for `delete`, just save the supporter being deleted).
- Cons: We must ensure that the implementation of each individual command is correct. For example, undoing `delete` must put the supporter back at the same position with all their interactions.
**Aspect: Where states are committed:**

- **Alternative 1 (current choice):** `ModelManager` marks the data as changed in `addPerson`, `setPerson`, `deletePerson` and `setAddressBook`, and `LogicManager` calls `Model#commitAddressBookIfChanged(String)` after every successful command.

- Pros: Commands that change data, such as `intro`, `tag` and `untag`, and later ones such as `editlog` and `unlog`, are undoable without any extra code, since every data change goes through those four methods. Commands that change nothing, such as `list` or a `stage` command that leaves the stage unchanged, create no undo step.
- Cons: A new `Model` method that changes data must also mark the data as changed. `UndoableCommandsTest` checks each data-changing command through `LogicManager`.
- **Alternative 2:** Each command that changes data calls a commit method itself.
- Pros: The commit is visible in each command's code.
- Cons: Every new command must remember to commit. Forgetting gives no error; undo just skips that command or reverts it together with the next one.
- **Alternative 3:** `LogicManager` commits after every successful command, without checking for changes.
- Pros: Simplest; no flag is needed.
- Cons: Read-only commands would create empty undo steps, so `undo` would sometimes appear to do nothing.
### Command history feature
#### Implementation

Pressing Up or Down in the command box brings back earlier commands. This is handled entirely in the `UI` component by `CommandHistory`, a plain Java class with no JavaFX code that `CommandBox` creates when it starts. `CommandHistory` keeps:
- `commands` -- the commands entered this session, oldest first.
- `cursor` -- the index of the command being shown, or `commands.size()` when the user is not browsing the history.
- `draft` -- the text that was in the command box when the user started browsing.
It offers three operations:
- `CommandHistory#add(String)` -- Records a command as the newest one and stops browsing. A blank command, or one identical to the newest command, is not stored again.

- `CommandHistory#previous(String)` -- Moves back one command and returns it. If the user was not browsing yet, the given text is kept as the draft first. It stays on the oldest command once it is reached, and returns an empty `Optional` if no commands have been entered.

- `CommandHistory#next()` -- Moves forward one command and returns it. Moving past the newest command returns the draft. If the user is already past the newest command, it returns an empty `Optional`, so text typed without browsing is kept.

`CommandBox` calls `add` when the user presses Enter, before the command is executed, so commands that fail are recorded too and can be corrected. It listens for key presses with an event filter on its text field. The sequence diagram below shows what happens when the user presses Up:
<puml src="diagrams/CommandHistorySequenceDiagram.puml" alt="CommandHistorySequenceDiagram" />

After showing the command, `CommandBox` consumes the key event, so the text field does not also move the caret to the start of the line. Down works the same way through `next()`, without the draft step.
Given below is an example of how the history changes:
Step 1. The user enters `list`, then `delete 1`. `commands` is `[list, delete 1]` and `cursor` is 2, past the newest command.

Step 2. The user types `find Al` but does not press Enter, then presses Up. As the user was not browsing yet, `previous("find Al")` keeps `find Al` as the draft, moves `cursor` to 1 and returns `delete 1`.
Step 3. The user presses Up again. `cursor` moves to 0 and `list` is shown. Pressing Up once more keeps `list`, as it is the oldest command.
Step 4. The user presses Down twice. The first press shows `delete 1`. The second moves `cursor` past the newest command, so `next()` returns the draft and `find Al` is back in the command box.
#### Design considerations:
**Aspect: Where the history is kept:**
- **Alternative 1 (current choice):** In `CommandHistory`, owned by `CommandBox` in the `UI` component.
- Pros: Recalling a command only changes the text in the command box, so `Logic` and `Model` are not involved. As plain Java, it is unit tested without starting JavaFX.
- Cons: Another part of the app, e.g. a future `history` command, could not list the commands without going through the UI.
- **Alternative 2:** In `Logic`, recording each command `LogicManager` receives.
- Pros: The history would be available to commands.
- Cons: `Logic` would hold state that only matters for typing, and a command that fails to parse would need extra handling to be recorded.
**Aspect: Whether the history is saved:**
- **Alternative 1 (current choice):** Kept in memory and cleared when the app closes.
- Pros: Simple, and commands, which can contain supporters' personal details in notes, are not written to another file.
- Cons: The user cannot recall commands from an earlier session.
- **Alternative 2:** Saved to a file and loaded at startup.
- Pros: Commands from earlier sessions can be recalled.
- Cons: Another file to read, write and keep safe, for a small convenience.

**Use case: UC01 - Add a supporter**
**MSS**
1.  User requests to add a supporter, giving their details.
2.  SupporterBook adds the supporter and shows the full list with the new supporter at the end.
Use case ends.

- 1a. User did not provide a name.
- 1a1. SupporterBook shows an error message.

- 1b. User provided neither a phone number nor an email.
- 1b1. SupporterBook shows an error message stating that at least one is required.
Use case resumes from step 1.
- 1c. User provided a detail that is invalid (e.g. a name with unsupported symbols, a phone number with unbalanced parentheses, an unknown stage).
- 1c1. SupporterBook shows an error message for that detail.
Use case resumes from step 1.
- 1d. A supporter with the same name already exists, ignoring capitalisation, extra spaces and differences between straight and curly apostrophes.
- 1d1. SupporterBook shows an error message suggesting a way to tell the two supporters apart.
Use case resumes from step 1.
- 1e. User gives more than one value for a detail that takes only one value (e.g. two names).
- 1e1. SupporterBook shows an error message, indicating the detail with multiple values given.

**MSS**
1.  User requests to list all supporters.
2.  SupporterBook shows the list of every supporter, clearing any find filter.

**Use case: UC03 - Find supporters by name or other fields**
**MSS**
1.  User requests to find supporters, giving name keywords, filters for organisation, tag, cultivation stage, phone number or email, or a combination of these.

2.  SupporterBook searches all supporters. Alternatives within the same field use OR; different fields use AND. Text matching ignores case and allows substrings, stages match complete stage names, and phone matching ignores formatting, labels and extension markers while retaining extension digits.

3.  SupporterBook shows the matches in their original full-list order, numbered from 1, and reports the number of matches. This replaces any previous find or quiet filter and sorting, without changing the viewed supporter or saved supporter data.
Use case ends.

- 1a. User did not provide any name keywords or field filters.
- 1a1. SupporterBook shows an error message with the correct command format, leaving the displayed list and viewed supporter unchanged.

- 1b. A field filter is empty, a cultivation stage is invalid, or a phone search value does not follow the accepted format.
- 1b1. SupporterBook shows the relevant error message, leaving the displayed list and viewed supporter unchanged.
Use case resumes from step 1.
- 1c. User supplies a filter reserved for another command, such as an address filter.
- 1c1. SupporterBook identifies the unsupported filter and shows the supported filters and correct command format, leaving the displayed list and viewed supporter unchanged.
Use case resumes from step 1.
- 3a. No supporter matches the combined criteria.
- 3a1. SupporterBook shows an empty list and reports zero matches, leaving the viewed supporter unchanged.

**Use case: UC14 - Find supporters who have gone quiet**
**MSS**
1.  User requests to find supporters needing follow-up, optionally specifying a number of days since last contact.

2.  SupporterBook searches all supporters using today's local date and the supplied threshold, or 60 days if none was supplied. It excludes supporters at the Declined stage and includes the others only if they have no interactions or their latest interaction was more than the threshold number of calendar days ago.

3.  SupporterBook shows never-contacted supporters first, then supporters with interactions ordered by their latest interaction date, oldest first. Ties retain full-list order. The results replace any previous find or quiet filter and sorting, and are numbered from 1.

- 3a. No supporter meets the quiet criteria.

### Non-Functional Requirements
1.  Should work on any _mainstream OS_ as long as it has Java `25` or above installed.
2.  Should work without requiring an installer.
3.  Should be distributable as a single JAR file of no more than 100 MB.
4.  Should be usable by a single user on one computer, without supporting concurrent or shared access to the same data.
5.  Should store all supporter data locally in a human-readable file that can be inspected and edited while the application is not running.
6.  Should be usable for its normal functionality without depending on a remote server or internet connection.
7.  Should clearly inform the user if supporter data cannot be loaded or saved, rather than failing silently.
8.  With up to 1000 supporters, each with up to 50 logged interactions, every command should complete within 1 second on a typical laptop.

9.  A user with above average typing speed for regular English text (i.e. not code, not system admin commands) should be able to accomplish most common supporter-management tasks faster using commands than using the mouse.
10. The GUI should work well at standard screen resolutions 1920x1080 or higher at 100% or 125% screen scaling, and should remain usable at resolutions 1280x720 or higher and 150% scaling.
11. Should not send any supporter data over the network, so that supporters' personal details stay on the user's computer.
12. Should not require the user to create an account or log in.
### Glossary
- **CRM (Customer Relationship Management system)**: Software that an organisation uses to keep track of its relationships with customers or supporters. Small charities often cannot afford one.

- **CSR (Corporate Social Responsibility)**: A company's programme for supporting causes such as charities, e.g. through donations, partnerships or employee volunteering. A _CSR contact_ is the person at a company who manages it.
- **Cultivation stage**: How far a supporter's relationship with the charity has progressed. Every supporter is at exactly one of these six stages:
- **Prospect**: Identified as a possible supporter, not yet approached. This is the default stage when `st/` is omitted from `add`.
- **Contacted**: First approach made, with no real conversation yet.
- **Cultivating**: In an active relationship or discussion, not yet giving.
- **Giving**: Currently donating (an individual) or partnering (a company).
- **Lapsed**: Gave before, but is no longer giving.
- **Declined**: Said no.
- **Epic**: A large user need that is broken down into several smaller user stories. The user stories above are grouped by epic.

- **Find filter**: The filtered list of supporters shown after a `find` or `quiet` command. It stays in place until another `find` or `quiet` replaces it, or `list`, `add`, `undo`, `redo` or an `edit` that changes something shows the full list again.
- **Index**: The number shown beside a supporter in the currently displayed list, used by commands to refer to that supporter. The same supporter can have a different index after a `find`.
- **Interaction**: A dated record of one conversation or other contact with a supporter, with a short note of what happened. A supporter's interactions together form their _interaction history_.
- **Introducer**: The supporter who introduced another supporter to the charity, recorded with `intro`. A supporter has at most one introducer, who must be another supporter in SupporterBook.
- **Introduction chain**: A sequence of introductions linking supporters, e.g. a board member introduces a CSR contact, who then introduces a colleague.
- **IPC (Institution of a Public Character)**: A Singapore charity that is approved to issue tax-deductible receipts to its donors.
- **Last contact**: The latest date among a supporter's interactions, whatever order they were logged in. A supporter with no interactions has no last contact.
- **Mainstream OS**: Windows, Linux, Unix, or macOS

- **Quiet supporter**: A supporter who may need a follow-up because they have no interactions, or their last contact was more than a given number of days ago (60 unless stated otherwise). Supporters at the `Declined` stage are never quiet. `quiet` lists them.

- **Supporter**: Anyone whose relationship with the charity SupporterBook keeps track of, e.g. an individual donor, a prospective donor, a contact at a partner company, a board member, or a volunteer who makes introductions.

- **Tier 1 charity**: Under the Code of Governance for Charities and IPCs (2023), a small or medium charity that is not an IPC, with gross annual receipts or total expenditure from $50,000 to under $10 million. Tier 2 covers all IPCs and large non-IPC charities.

# SupporterBook User Guide

SupporterBook is a **desktop application for fundraising and outreach staff at small charities to manage donor and corporate supporter relationships, optimised for use through a Command Line Interface (CLI)** while retaining the benefits of a Graphical User Interface (GUI). It keeps supporter details, cultivation stages and interaction histories in one place. If you type quickly, SupporterBook can help you find and update supporter records faster than traditional GUI applications.
<!-- * Table of Contents -->
<page-nav-print />
## Quick start
1. Ensure that Java `25` or later is installed on your computer.
**Mac users:** Ensure you have the precise JDK version prescribed [here](https://se-education.org/guides/tutorials/javaInstallationMac.html).
1. Download the latest `supporterbook.jar` file from [here](https://github.com/AY2627S1-CS2103T-T14-2/tp/releases).

1. Copy the file to an empty folder you want to use as the _home folder_ for SupporterBook. Your data is saved in a `data` folder inside it, so choose a folder where you can create files (not a read-only folder).
1. Open a terminal, `cd` to the folder containing the JAR file, and run `java -jar "supporterbook.jar"`.

Use this command rather than double-clicking the JAR file. Double-clicking may start the app with a different Java version, and the app saves its data relative to the folder it is started from, so it may not find or save your data in the home folder.
A GUI similar to the one below should appear in a few seconds. Note how the app contains some sample supporters. A few already have logged interactions, which you can see with `view`.
![Ui](images/Ui.png)
1. Type a command in the command box and press Enter to execute it. For example, type **`help`** and press Enter to open the help window.
Some example commands you can try:
- `list` : Lists all supporters.
- `add n/Tan Wei Ming p/91234567 e/weiming@dbs.com o/DBS Bank` : Adds a supporter named `Tan Wei Ming` from `DBS Bank`.
- `log 1 nt/Called about the year-end appeal` : Logs an interaction with the 1st supporter shown in the current list.
- `view 1` : Shows the 1st supporter's interaction history.
- `stage 1 contacted` : Sets the 1st supporter's cultivation stage to `Contacted`.
- `delete 3` : Deletes the 3rd supporter shown in the current list, together with their interactions.
- `exit` : Exits the app.
1. Refer to the [Features](#features) section below for details of each command.
## Features
<box type="info" seamless>
**Notes about the command format:**
- Words in `UPPER_CASE` are the parameters to be supplied by the user.
For example, in `add n/NAME`, replace `NAME` with a value such as `John Doe`.
- Command words ignore case. For example, `list`, `LIST` and `List` all list every supporter.

- Supporter and interaction numbers must be positive whole numbers written with the digits `0` to `9`. Use the supporter number in the currently displayed list and the interaction number shown beside the entry. Leading zeros are allowed (`01` means `1`), but other digit characters, such as full-width `１`, are rejected.
- Items in square brackets are optional.
For example, `n/NAME [t/TAG]` can be used as `n/John Doe t/friend` or as `n/John Doe`.
- Items followed by `...` can appear zero or more times.
For example, `[t/TAG]... ` may be omitted, or written as `t/friend` or `t/friend t/family`.
- Prefixed parameters can be in any order among themselves. Parameters without prefixes must stay in the positions shown in the command format.
For example, `edit 1 n/John Doe p/91234567` and `edit 1 p/91234567 n/John Doe` are equivalent, but `INDEX` must remain before the prefixed parameters.
For `find`, name keywords must come before the first prefix; its prefixed filters can be in any order.

- A command only recognises the prefixes in its own format. Other prefix-like words normally stay part of the value before them, e.g. `em/` mistyped for `e/`, or `e/` used in `log`. The exception is `find`: known prefixes outside its search format are rejected with an unsupported-search-filter error. Other prefix-like words are not automatically rejected, since addresses and notes can contain slashes, e.g. `Unit/3`.

For words treated as ordinary text, SupporterBook adds an advisory note in the cases below. This includes prefixes that belong to another command, e.g. `by/` in `add`, `st/` in `edit` or `t/` in `log`:

- If the command saves the word, e.g. into an address or a note, the note follows the result, so you can run `undo` and enter the command again. For example, `log 1 nt/Called dte/2024-10-01` logs the note `Called dte/2024-10-01` dated today, and points out `dte/`.

- If the command's format or one of its values is invalid, the note follows the error, as the mistyped prefix may be what made the value before it invalid. For example, `add n/Tan p/91234567 by/1` shows the rules for phone numbers, followed by `Note: by/ is not a recognised prefix for this command, so it was read as part of the value before it.`

- If the format and values are valid but the command still cannot be carried out, only the error is shown. For example, `log 999 nt/Called dte/2024-10-01` with fewer than 999 supporters displayed reports the out-of-range supporter index without a note.
Everyday words such as `s/o`, `c/o`, `w/` and `and/or` are not flagged. If a note points out a word you meant to type, such as `Unit/` in an address, you can ignore it.

- Extraneous parameters for commands that take no parameters, such as `help`, `list`, `stats`, `exit` and `clear`, are ignored. `undo` and `redo` instead reject any parameters, so that `undo 3` cannot look like it undid three changes.
For example, `help 123` is interpreted as `help`. Prefix-like words in these ignored parameters do not produce a note.
- For the rules each parameter must follow, see the [Parameter summary](#parameter-summary).

- If you are using a PDF version of this document, be careful when copying and pasting commands that span multiple lines as space characters surrounding line-breaks may be omitted when copied over to the application.
</box>
### Viewing help: `help`
Opens a help window with a link to this user guide.
![help message](images/helpMessage.png)
Format: `help`
- You can also open the help window with the `Help` menu or by pressing `F1`.
- Click **Copy URL** to copy the user guide's link. The button shows `Copied!` for 2 seconds to confirm the link was copied.
### Adding a supporter: `add`
Adds a supporter to SupporterBook.
Format: `add n/NAME [p/PHONE] [e/EMAIL] [a/ADDRESS] [o/ORGANISATION] [st/STAGE] [t/TAG]... `
- At least one of `p/PHONE` and `e/EMAIL` must be given, so that there is a way to reach the supporter. Online donors often give only an email, and people met at events often give only a number.
- `a/ADDRESS` can be left out, e.g. when you do not know a corporate contact's postal address.

- To leave out a field the supporter does not have, leave out its prefix too. A prefix with nothing after it, e.g. `e/` on its own, is rejected with a message saying which field is blank. (In `edit`, an empty prefix clears the field instead.)
- `ORGANISATION` is the company or group the supporter belongs to, e.g. the company a CSR contact speaks for. Leave out `o/ORGANISATION` for individual donors.

- `ORGANISATION` can include text, punctuation and emoji (e.g. `Procter & Gamble`). A space followed by a recognised command prefix such as `a/` or `t/` starts another field. For example, in `Bang & Olufsen a/s`, `a/` is interpreted as the address prefix.

- `ORGANISATION` must not be blank and can be at most 100 characters long after leading and trailing spaces are removed and repeated internal spaces are reduced to one. For this limit, simple emoji such as 😀 count as one character, while combined emoji or a letter with a combining accent can count as more than one.
- Each supporter card in the list shows the supporter's organisation, or `(no organisation)` if they have none.
- `EMAIL` must be of the form `local-part@domain`. The local part can contain English letters, digits
and the special characters `+`, `_`, `-` and `.`, e.g. `wei_ming+donations@dbs.com`. A period cannot
start or end the local part, or appear twice in a row. The domain is made up of at least two labels
separated by periods, e.g. `dbs.com` or `u.nus.edu`. Each label must start and end with an English letter
or digit and may contain internal hyphens, including consecutive hyphens. ASCII forms of internationalised
domains, e.g. `contact@xn--bcher-kva.de`, are accepted. The final label, e.g. `com` or `sg`, must have at
least two characters and contain only English letters, so `a@bc` and `123@145.67` are rejected.
- `STAGE` is the supporter's cultivation stage, and must be one of `prospect`, `contacted`, `cultivating`, `giving`, `lapsed` or `declined`. Upper and lower case are both accepted.
- If `st/STAGE` is left out, the new supporter starts at stage `Prospect`.
- `PHONE` may start with `+` and must contain between 3 and 15 main-number digits.
Digit groups may be separated by single spaces or hyphens, including a mixture of both.
A digit group may be enclosed in balanced parentheses, e.g. `(65) 9123 4567`.
Consecutive separators such as `+65  9123` or `+65- 9123` are not accepted.
- A phone number may end with `ext` followed by 1 to 6 extension digits and/or an alphabetic
label in parentheses, with single spaces between parts. `ext` is case-insensitive.
If both are supplied, the extension comes before the label, e.g. `9123 4567 ext 12 (Office)`.
Labels contain English letters, optionally separated by single spaces, e.g. `(HP)`, `(Home)`
and `(Office Fax)`. Extension digits do not count towards the main number's 3-to-15-digit limit.
Your formatting, including the extension and label, is preserved when displayed and saved.

- `NAME` must start with a letter or digit, and can contain letters, digits, spaces, apostrophes (`'` or `’`), hyphens (`-`), periods (`.`), commas (`,`), round brackets (`(` and `)`) and at signs (`@`), e.g. `O'Brien`, `Lee-Tan`, `J. Tan`, `Tan, Ah Kow`, `Tan Ah Kow (Chen Ah Kow)` and `Ahmad bin Ali @ Ah Mat`.

- Accented and non-Latin letters, including letters with combining marks, are accepted in `NAME`, e.g. `José Tan`, `கவி` and `李伟` (on some computers, names in scripts such as Tamil may not display correctly; see [Known issues](#known-issues)). Combining accents and other marks must be attached to a letter; they cannot appear on their own or after a digit, space or punctuation.
- `NAME` can also contain `s/o` or `d/o` as separate words, e.g. `Ravi s/o Kumar` and `Priya d/o Kumar`. Upper and lower case are both accepted.
- SupporterBook only checks which characters a name uses, not whether it looks like a real name. For example, `s/o Kumar` or a name with only initials is accepted.

- Round brackets in `NAME` do not need to be balanced, and spaces around punctuation are optional. The name must still start with a letter or digit, so `(Tan)` and `@Tan` are rejected. These name rules apply to both `add` and `edit`.
- Extra spaces in `NAME` are removed, e.g. `n/  Tan   Wei Ming` is saved as `Tan Wei Ming`. Non-breaking spaces, often copied from web pages, are treated as ordinary spaces too.

- Two supporters cannot have the same name. Names are compared ignoring capital letters and extra spaces, so `tan wei ming` is the same supporter as `Tan Wei Ming`. Typing an accented letter directly or adding its accent separately also counts as the same name. If two different people share a name, add something to tell them apart, e.g. `n/Tan Wei Ming DBS`.

- Straight (`'`) and curly (`’`) apostrophes also count as the same character when comparing names, so `Charlotte O'Brien` and `Charlotte O’Brien` count as the same supporter. The apostrophe style you enter is preserved when the name is saved and displayed.
- `TAG` must be alphanumeric, with no spaces, e.g. `t/boardIntro`. Tags that differ only in capitalisation, e.g. `t/vip t/VIP`, count as one tag, and the spelling typed first is kept.
- After adding, the list shows all supporters in the order they were added (any `find` or `quiet` filter is cleared), with the new supporter at the bottom.
If another supporter has the same phone number or email, the addition still succeeds, but a
warning names the existing supporters and identifies the shared fields. Shared contact details
may be legitimate, so the warning does not block saving. Check the named records before deciding
whether to keep or undo the addition.
Phone comparison uses the complete number, ignoring formatting; country codes are not inferred,
so `+65 9123-4567` and `6591234567` match, but `91234567` is not assumed to be the same number.
Email comparison ignores case but does not remove dots or `+suffixes`.
The check includes supporters hidden by `find` or `quiet`. It applies when adding or editing,
not when loading existing data, and does not change the rule that duplicate names are rejected.
For example, if Alex Yeoh already has phone `87438807`, `add n/Dup Phone p/87438807` still adds
the new supporter and includes a warning identifying `Alex Yeoh (phone)`.

- At least one of the optional fields must be provided.
- Existing values will be updated to the input values. Each value follows the same rules as in `add`.

- If the supporter already has all the given values, e.g. `edit 1 n/Alex Yeoh` for a supporter already named `Alex Yeoh`, the command reports `Nothing was changed.` and leaves the list and undo/redo history unchanged, so a following `undo` reverses an earlier change, if one is available.

- To remove all of a supporter's tags, enter `t/` without a tag after it.
- To clear a supporter's address or organisation, enter `a/` or `o/` with nothing after it.

- To clear a supporter's phone number or email, enter `p/` or `e/` with nothing after it. This works only if the supporter keeps the other one, since every supporter needs a way to be reached. You can clear one and give a new value for the other in the same command, e.g. `edit 1 e/ p/91234567`.
- A supporter's name cannot be cleared.
- A supporter's stage cannot be changed with `edit`, and stays the same when other details are edited. Use the `stage` command instead.
- A supporter's logged interactions are kept when their details are edited.
- A supporter's introducer is kept when their details are edited. If you rename a supporter who introduced others, those supporters show the new name as their introducer.
- A supporter's name cannot be changed to the name of another supporter, using the same comparison as `add`. Changing only the capitalisation of their own name is allowed.

- If an edit that changes something leaves the record sharing a phone number or email with another supporter, the edit still succeeds and a warning names the matching supporters and fields, using the same comparison rules as `add`. Hidden supporters are included, but the edited supporter is not compared with their own original record. The warning reflects the resulting record, including contact details you did not change; check whether the sharing is intentional before keeping or undoing the edit.

### Finding supporters by name or other fields: `find`
Finds supporters by name, organisation, tag, stage, phone number or email. Combine fields to narrow a search.
Format: `find [NAME_KEYWORD]... [o/ORG]... [t/TAG]... [st/STAGE]... [p/PHONE]... [e/EMAIL]...`
Supply at least one name keyword or nonempty prefix value. Name keywords are optional when a field filter is given.
| Search field | Input | Matching rule |
| Name | `NAME_KEYWORD` | Case-insensitive substring; `wei` matches `Tan Wei Ming` and `Weiling Koh` |
| Organisation | `o/ORG` | Case-insensitive substring; `o/dbs` matches `DBS Bank` |
| Tag | `t/TAG` | Case-insensitive substring of any tag; `t/board` matches `boardIntro` |
| Stage | `st/STAGE` | Complete stage name, ignoring case; `st/GIVING` matches `Giving`, but `st/giv` is invalid |
| Phone | `p/PHONE` | Digit substring after ignoring formatting, a trailing type label and the `ext` marker; extension digits remain searchable |
| Email | `e/EMAIL` | Case-insensitive substring; `e/@gmail` matches an address containing `@gmail` |

- Text searches ignore case and treat straight (`'`) and curly (`’`) apostrophes as the same character. For example, both `find O'Brien` and `find O’Brien` match `Charlotte O'Brien` and `Eleanor O’Brien`. The same rule applies to organisation searches.

- Typing an accented letter directly or adding its accent separately produces the same search results for names and organisations. Accents remain significant, so `Jose` does not match `José`. Searching preserves the spelling saved in each supporter record.
- **OR within a field:** any name keyword can match, and repeated values of a prefix are alternatives. For example, `find st/giving st/lapsed` finds supporters at either stage.

- **AND between fields:** every specified field must match. For example, `find tan o/DBS st/giving` finds supporters whose names contain `tan`, whose organisation contains `DBS`, and whose stage is `Giving`.

- To find supporters who match either of two different fields, e.g. everyone at DBS or everyone tagged `csr`, run one `find` for each field, e.g. `find o/DBS`, then `find t/csr`. Each `find` replaces the previous result rather than adding to it, so check the supporters shown after each one; the two results are not combined into one list.
- Repeating an identical value does not duplicate supporters or change the matches.
- Name keywords must appear before the first prefix, without quotation marks. Use `find tan o/DBS Bank`, not `find o/DBS Bank tan`: the latter searches for the organisation text `DBS Bank tan`.

- Prefixes used by other commands (`n/`, `a/`, `dt/`, `nt/` and `by/`) are rejected anywhere in a search. The error lists each unsupported prefix, states that `find` supports only `o/`, `t/`, `st/`, `p/` and `e/`, and includes the usage message. Use `find alex` to search by name; `find n/alex`, `find a/geylang` and `find o/dbs a/geylang` are rejected.

- Prefix values may contain multiple words. Each prefix value is one search phrase; `o/DBS Bank` searches for that phrase. Name keywords are separated by whitespace and use OR; `weiming` does not match `Wei Ming`.

- Non-breaking spaces (NBSPs, U+00A0) pasted into search criteria are treated like ordinary spaces. Repeated ordinary spaces or NBSPs are reduced to one space, and leading or trailing ones are ignored. For example, `find Tan Wei Ming` and `find o/DBS Bank` return the same results when the spaces between the name or organisation words are NBSPs.
- Prefixed filters can appear in any order. To provide alternatives, repeat the prefix: use `st/giving st/lapsed`, not `st/giving lapsed`.
- Phone queries follow the phone format above, but the main-number length limit does not apply.
and `p/4567 ext 12` matches `9123 4567 ext 12 (Office)`.
Formatting, the `ext` marker and type labels are ignored; the main and extension digits form
the searchable digit sequence. Queries must contain main-number digits: `p/+` and `p/(HP)`
are rejected. Labels cannot be searched by themselves using `p/`.
- A supporter without an organisation, phone number, email or tags does not match a search on that missing field.
- Results stay in their original list order and are numbered from 1. Other commands use these displayed indices.
- A new `find` searches all supporters and replaces the previous filter. `list`, `add`, `undo`, `redo` and an `edit` that changes something show the full list again.
- Searching preserves the viewed supporter, even when they are absent from the results. It does not change saved supporter data or add an undo point, and it preserves redo history.
- `find` without criteria and empty filters such as `o/` are rejected. Invalid stage names produce the stage error message. Invalid searches leave the previous results unchanged.
For a list containing `Tan Wei Ming`, `Tan Ah Kow` and `Weiling Koh`:
- `find wei` returns `Tan Wei Ming` and `Weiling Koh`.
- `find tan wei` returns all three supporters.
- `find KOH` returns `Weiling Koh`.
- `find tan tan` returns the same results as `find tan`.
Other examples:
- `find o/DBS Bank` finds supporters whose organisation contains `DBS Bank`.
- `find t/board t/donor` finds supporters with a tag containing either `board` or `donor`.
- `find st/giving st/lapsed e/@example.com` finds supporters at either stage whose email contains `@example.com`.
- `find tan lim o/DBS o/OCBC st/giving` means `(name contains tan OR lim) AND (organisation contains DBS OR OCBC) AND (stage is Giving)`.
The success message reports the number of matches, for example `3 supporter(s) listed!`.
If nothing matches, the list is empty and the message is `0 supporter(s) listed!`.
Run `list` to show all supporters again.
### Finding supporters who have gone quiet: `quiet`
Shows supporters needing follow-up, starting with those who have gone longest without contact.
Format: `quiet [DAYS]`
- `quiet` uses a threshold of 60 days. Supply a positive whole number to change it, e.g. `quiet 30`.
- Supporters with no interactions are included. Supporters at stage `Declined` are excluded, even if they have no interactions.

- A supporter with interactions is included only if their most recent interaction was **more than** `DAYS` calendar days ago. Someone contacted exactly 60 days ago is excluded from `quiet 60`; someone contacted 61 days ago is included.
- Last contact is the latest interaction date, regardless of logging order. Logging an older interaction does not replace a more recent last-contact date.
- Supporters with no interactions appear first, followed by the oldest last-contact date. Ties retain the order in which supporters appear in the full list.
- The date is taken from the computer's local clock when you run the command. Rerun `quiet` to refresh the threshold after the date changes.
- Each `quiet` searches all supporters and replaces the previous filter and ordering. It does not narrow a previous `find` result.
- Other commands use the numbers in this displayed list. For example, `quiet` followed by `view 1` opens the first quiet supporter, and `delete 1` deletes that supporter.

- Changes to interactions or stages refresh the quiet list. Logging recent contact can remove a supporter; deleting their last interaction can move them to the top. Check the displayed indices again after a change.

- `list` restores the full list in its normal order. `find` restores normal ordering for its matching results. Successful `add`, `undo` and `redo`, and an `edit` that changes something, also restore the full list in normal order.
- Running `quiet` preserves the viewed supporter, supporter data and saved order. It adds no undo point and preserves redo history.
- Supply at most one day count, from `1` to `2147483647`. Zero, negatives, decimals, non-numbers, larger values and additional arguments are rejected without changing the current list or selection.
Examples:
- `quiet` lists eligible supporters with no interactions or last contact more than 60 days ago.
- `quiet 30` uses a shorter threshold for more frequent follow-up.
- `quiet 90` followed by `view 1` opens the first supporter in that result.
- `list` restores the normal list when you finish reviewing quiet supporters.
The success message reports the count and threshold, for example:
```text
3 supporter(s) listed: no interactions or last contacted more than 60 days ago.
No matches produces an empty list and the same message with a count of `0`.

Permanently removes the specified supporter together with every interaction logged with them.

- Deletes the supporter at the specified `INDEX`, including their entire interaction history.
- The index refers to the index number shown in the displayed supporter list, including after `find`.
- The index **must be a positive integer** 1, 2, 3, ...
- The success message reports the number of interactions removed, including `0` when there were none. Identical entries are counted separately.
- The current find filter is retained, and supporters below the deleted entry move up one number.
- If the supporter is shown in the detail panel, their details and history are cleared and the startup prompt returns. Deleting another supporter preserves the panel's displayed supporter.
- Other supporters' details and interaction histories are unchanged, including notes that mention the deleted supporter.
- If the deleted supporter introduced others, they are removed as those supporters' introducer, and the success message says how many supporters this affected.

### Logging an interaction: `log`
Records an interaction with a supporter, dated today or on a specified past date.
Format: `log INDEX nt/NOTE [dt/DATE]`
- Logs the interaction against the supporter at the specified `INDEX`. The index refers to the index number shown in the displayed supporter list and must be a positive integer.

- `NOTE` records what happened and can include text, punctuation and emoji. It must not be blank and can be at most 500 characters long. Leading and trailing spaces are removed. For this limit, simple emoji such as 😀 count as one character, while combined emoji or a letter with a combining accent can count as more than one.
- Without `dt/`, the date defaults to today when the command runs, using the computer's clock.

- `DATE` must be a valid date in `yyyy-MM-dd` format, e.g. `2024-02-29`, from `1900-01-01` through today (inclusive). Empty or out-of-range dates are rejected. Today is determined by the computer's clock.
- `nt/` and `dt/` can appear in either order. Each prefix may only be supplied once.
- Each supporter's oldest interaction is `#1`; the newest has the largest number. On equal dates, the later-logged entry has the larger number and appears first.
- Back-dating can renumber existing entries; entry numbers are not permanent IDs.
- Identical notes logged on the same day are accepted as separate interactions.
- The success message shows the supporter, date, note and entry number matching the panel.
- The panel switches to this supporter and displays entries newest first.

- Logging an interaction does not change the supporter's cultivation stage or clear the active list filter. A `find` result remains in place; a `quiet` result updates to reflect the new last-contact date, so the supporter may move or disappear from the result.
<box type="warning" seamless>
A space followed by `nt/` or `dt/` inside a note is interpreted as a parameter prefix, not note text. This may split the note or cause a validation error. Rephrase the note to avoid these sequences.
</box>
Examples:
- `log 2 nt/Coffee at Raffles Place, keen on a Q4 volunteering day`
- `log 2 nt/Meeting entered later dt/2024-02-29` records a meeting on 29 February 2024.
- `find Bernice` followed by `log 1 nt/Left voicemail about the year-end appeal` logs the interaction against the 1st supporter in the search results.
Logging 10 March, then 20 February, then 29 February 2024 gives:

#3  10 Mar 2024  Recent call
#2  29 Feb 2024  Middle meeting
#1  20 Feb 2024  First meeting
The last command reports `#2`. Adding that entry renumbers the 10 March entry from `#2` to `#3`.

Shows a supporter's full record and every logged interaction in the detail panel beside the supporter list. The result display reports their name and interaction count.

* `INDEX` is required and must be a positive integer from the currently displayed supporter list. After a `find`, use the index shown in the search results.
* Supply exactly one index, with no additional arguments.
* Viewing a supporter preserves the displayed list, its filter and all supporter data.

* The panel shows the name, stage, organisation, phone, email, address, tags, introducer and the supporters they introduced. Unset fields, including an empty tag list, appear as `-`. Tags are shown alphabetically, ignoring capitalisation, in the same order as on the supporter card and in command results.

* Above the interaction history, the panel shows the same last-contact line as the supporter card, for example `Last contact: 03 Oct 2026`, or `No interactions yet` if there are no logged interactions. The line updates when the displayed supporter's interaction history changes.
* Interactions appear newest first, e.g. `#4  16 Sep 2026  Sent partnership deck by email`. Numbers descend to `#1`, the oldest entry. On equal dates, later-logged entries appear first.
* If the window is too short to show everything, the panel gets a scroll bar, so you can scroll down to the interaction history.

* The panel keeps showing the supporter while you run `list`, `find` or `add`, even if that supporter disappears from the displayed list. These commands also preserve the current history scroll position.

* After `undo` or `redo`, the panel shows the displayed supporter's restored record, or is cleared if that supporter no longer exists.
* Selection is not remembered after restarting the app.
* Clicking a supporter card does not select it or change the panel. Use `view INDEX` to show a supporter.

### Recording who introduced a supporter: `intro`

Records which supporter introduced another, e.g. the board member who introduced you to a company's CSR lead. This lets you see whose goodwill created each relationship, and everyone a given person has introduced you to.
Format: `intro INDEX by/[INTRODUCER_INDEX]`

- `INDEX` is the supporter who was introduced, and `INTRODUCER_INDEX` is the supporter who introduced them. Both refer to the index numbers shown in the displayed supporter list and **must be positive integers** 1, 2, 3, ...
- Both supporters must be in the displayed list. If one of them is hidden by a `find` filter, use `find` with both names, e.g. `find bernice charlotte`, or run `list` first.
- Running `intro` again for the same supporter replaces their introducer. Each supporter has at most one introducer.
- Leave out `INTRODUCER_INDEX` to remove the record, e.g. `intro 3 by/`.
- A supporter cannot be their own introducer.

- Introductions cannot go in a circle. If a supporter introduced someone, directly or through other supporters, that person cannot be recorded as their introducer. For example, if Alex introduced Bernice, and Bernice introduced David, then neither Bernice nor David can be recorded as Alex's introducer.
- If nothing would change (the same introducer again, or removing a record that does not exist), a message says so and the record is unchanged.
- On success, the detail panel switches to the introduced supporter. The displayed list stays the same, so a `find` result is kept.
- The detail panel shows each supporter's `Introducer`, and under `Introduced`, everyone they introduced.
- Renaming an introducer with `edit` keeps their introductions. Deleting an introducer removes them as the introducer of everyone they introduced.
Examples:
- `intro 3 by/1` records that the 1st supporter in the displayed list introduced the 3rd.
- `find bernice charlotte` followed by `intro 2 by/1` records that the 1st supporter in the search results introduced the 2nd.
- `intro 4 by/` removes the 4th supporter's introducer.

- Tags the supporter already has are skipped. Capital letters are ignored when checking, so `t/vip` is skipped if the supporter is tagged `VIP`, and the existing tag keeps its capitalisation.

Examples:
- `tag 2 t/vip` adds the tag `vip` to the 2nd supporter in the displayed list.
- `find David` followed by `tag 1 t/boardIntro t/gala2026` adds two tags to the 1st supporter in the search results.
### Removing tags from a supporter: `untag`
Removes one or more tags from a supporter, keeping their other tags.
Format: `untag INDEX t/TAG [t/TAG]...`
- Removes tags from the supporter at the specified `INDEX`. The index refers to the index number shown in the displayed supporter list and **must be a positive integer** 1, 2, 3, ...
- At least one `t/TAG` must be given. Each `TAG` must be alphanumeric, with no spaces, as in `add`.
- Capital letters are ignored, so `untag 1 t/vip` removes the tag `VIP`.
- Tags the supporter does not have are skipped.
- The result display lists the tags removed and the tags skipped. If every tag is skipped, nothing is changed and a message says so.

- On success, the detail panel switches to this supporter. The current list filter remains active, but removing a tag can remove the supporter from a `find` result if they no longer match. Check the displayed indices again before another command.
- To remove all of a supporter's tags at once, use `edit INDEX t/`.
Examples:
- `untag 2 t/csr` removes the tag `csr` from the 2nd supporter in the displayed list.
- `untag 2 t/csr t/boardIntro` removes two tags from the 2nd supporter.
- `find t/csr` followed by `untag 1 t/csr` removes the tag `csr` from the 1st supporter in the search results, who then no longer appears in them.
### Clearing all entries: `clear`
Deletes all supporters, together with their logged interactions.
Format: `clear`
- The list becomes empty, and the detail panel stops showing a supporter.
- If there are no supporters, nothing is changed and the result says so, so a following `undo` reverses an earlier change, if one is available.
- There is no confirmation prompt. If you clear the list by mistake, run [`undo`](#undoing-a-change-undo) straight away to restore every supporter.
### Undoing a change: `undo`
Reverts the most recent change to your supporter data.
Format: `undo`
- These commands can be undone: `add`, `edit`, `delete`, `clear`, `log`, `editlog`, `unlog`, `stage`, `intro`, `tag` and `untag`.
- Commands that do not change data, such as `list`, `find`, `view`, `stats` and `help`, are skipped. For example, `delete 2`, `find Tan`, `undo` restores the deleted supporter.
- Running `undo` again reverts the change before that, back to when the app was opened.

- A command that changes nothing, such as `stage` with the supporter's current stage, `tag` with a tag they already have, `edit` with the details they already have, `editlog` with the note and date the entry already has or `clear` when the list is already empty, is not recorded. Neither is a command that fails. There is nothing to undo for them.
- After undoing, all supporters are listed. The detail panel shows the displayed supporter's restored record, or is cleared if that supporter no longer exists.
- The result display names the command that made the change, as you typed it, e.g. `Undid the last change: tag 1 t/vip`.
- `undo` takes no parameters and undoes one change at a time. For example, `undo 3` is rejected and nothing is undone; enter `undo` three times instead.
- Undo history is kept only while the app is open. After you restart the app, earlier changes cannot be undone.
If there is nothing to undo, the result display shows `There is no change to undo.` and nothing is changed.
Examples:
- `delete 2` followed by `undo` restores the deleted supporter and their interaction history.
- `clear` followed by `undo` restores every supporter.
### Redoing an undone change: `redo`
Re-applies the change most recently reverted by `undo`.
Format: `redo`
- Running `redo` again re-applies the next undone change. Changes are redone in the order they were first made, so the change undone last is redone first.
- Making a new change after `undo` discards the undone changes, so they can no longer be redone.
- After redoing, all supporters are listed, and the detail panel is updated in the same way as for `undo`.
- The result display names the command being redone, e.g. `Redid the last undone change: tag 1 t/vip`.
- `redo` takes no parameters and redoes one change at a time, so `redo 3` is rejected and nothing is redone.
If there is nothing to redo, the result display shows `There is no undone change to redo.` and nothing is changed.
Examples:
- `delete 2`, `undo`, then `redo` deletes the same supporter again.
- `delete 2`, `undo`, then `log 1 nt/Called` means the delete can no longer be redone.
### Exiting the program: `exit`
Exits the program.
Format: `exit`
### Recalling previous commands

Press <kbd>Up</kbd> in the command box to bring back the commands you have entered, newest first, so that you can run a similar command again without retyping it. Press <kbd>Down</kbd> to move forward again.
- Every command you entered is remembered, including commands that failed, so you can fix a typo and try again.
- Pressing <kbd>Up</kbd> at the oldest command keeps it in the box.

- Pressing <kbd>Down</kbd> past the newest command brings back what you were typing before you first pressed <kbd>Up</kbd>, so an unfinished command is not lost. If the box was empty, it is left empty.
- Pressing <kbd>Down</kbd> while typing a new command, without having pressed <kbd>Up</kbd>, keeps what you typed.
- Entering the same command several times in a row stores it only once.
- The command history is cleared when you close the app. It is not saved to the data file.
Example: after `log 2 nt/Called about the gala`, press <kbd>Up</kbd>, change the index and note, and press <kbd>Enter</kbd> to log a similar interaction with another supporter.
### Saving the data
SupporterBook automatically saves data after every command that executes successfully. You do not need to save manually.

If saving fails, e.g. because the data file or its folder is read-only, the error says why. If the command changed the data, the error first shows the command's result, and the change is kept but not saved, so do not repeat the command: repeating `delete 1`, for example, would delete another supporter. Once the problem is fixed, run any command, e.g. `list`, to save all changes, or run `undo` to reverse the change (`redo` if the command that failed to save was `undo`). Changes that are not saved are lost when you close SupporterBook.
### Loading data at startup
SupporterBook loads `data/supporterbook.json` from the folder the app is launched from. The data file path is shown in the status bar.
* If the file is missing, the app starts with sample supporters. The file is created after the first command that executes successfully.
* If the file is valid, the app loads its supporters and lists them all.
* If the file cannot be loaded, the app starts with an empty list and shows a warning in the result display:

> Could not load data/supporterbook.json because it is not in the expected format. Starting with an empty list. Your next command will overwrite the file, so copy it somewhere safe now if you want to repair it.

The message includes the path of the file that could not be loaded. Invalid JSON, missing required fields, invalid field values, duplicate supporters, an introducer who is not in the file or introductions that go in a circle can cause this warning.

Startup does not overwrite the unreadable file. Copy it somewhere safe before running another command if you want to recover its contents. Even `list` saves data after executing, so it can replace the file with the empty list. A command that fails parsing or validation does not overwrite it.
The next command's result or error replaces the startup warning in the display. To repair the file, close the app, correct the copied data using the rules below, and restore it before relaunching.
### Editing the data file
SupporterBook data is saved as a JSON file `data/supporterbook.json`, relative to the folder the app is launched from. Advanced users can edit that file while the app is closed.

Each supporter in the data file has a `"stage"`, which records how far the relationship has progressed. It must be one of `Prospect`, `Contacted`, `Cultivating`, `Giving`, `Lapsed` or `Declined` (upper or lower case). A supporter's stage stays the same when you edit their other details.
A supporter's `"phone"`, `"email"` and `"address"` keys can each be left out if the supporter does not have one, but every supporter must have at least one of `"phone"` and `"email"`.

A supporter may also have an `"organisation"`, such as the company a CSR contact works for. Leave the key out if the supporter has no organisation. If present, it must not be blank and must contain at most 100 characters after leading and trailing spaces are removed and repeated internal spaces are reduced to one (see [how organisation characters are counted](#adding-a-supporter-add)).

A supporter may also have an `"introducer"`, the name of the supporter who introduced them, e.g. a board member. Leave the key out if no introducer is recorded. If present, it must be the name of another supporter in the same file, compared in the same way as names in `add` (capital letters and extra spaces are ignored, and straight and curly apostrophes count as the same), and cannot be the supporter's own name. Introductions in the file cannot go in a circle, e.g. Alex introduced by Bernice while Bernice is introduced by Alex.

A supporter's `"tags"` array lists their tags, each of which must be alphanumeric. Tags that differ only in capitalisation count as one tag, as they do in commands: if the file has both `"vip"` and `"VIP"`, only the one that comes first is loaded, and the other is removed the next time SupporterBook saves.
A supporter's `"interactions"` array stores entries in logging order.

Each entry has a `"date"` that must be a valid calendar date in `yyyy-MM-dd` format, from `1900-01-01` through tomorrow (inclusive) when loading. Today and tomorrow are determined by the computer's local clock when the file is loaded. This one-day allowance lets a previously saved interaction load when a time-zone change makes its date appear to be tomorrow. The stored date is kept unchanged. Dates entered through `log` and `editlog` must still be on or before today, as these commands record completed interactions.

Each entry also has a `"note"` that must not be blank and must contain at most 500 characters after leading and trailing spaces are removed (see [how note characters are counted](#logging-an-interaction-log)).
For example:
```json
"interactions" : [ {
"note" : "Called to discuss the year-end appeal"
The array may be empty or left out when the supporter has no interactions. A missing array is also how data files created before interaction histories were introduced remain compatible.
<box type="warning" seamless>
**Caution:**

If your changes make the data file invalid (e.g., a supporter's `"stage"` is missing or is not one of the six stages, or an interaction date is before `1900-01-01` or more than one day after today), SupporterBook starts with an empty list and shows the startup warning described above. Back up the file before editing it, and preserve the invalid file before running another command if you need to repair it.
Edit the data file only if you are confident that you can follow the validation rules.

## FAQ
**Q**: How do I transfer my data to another computer?
**A**: Install the app on the other computer and overwrite the data file it creates with the data file from your previous SupporterBook home folder.
## Known issues

1. **If you minimize the Help Window** and then run the `help` command (or use the `Help` menu, or the keyboard shortcut `F1`) again, the original Help Window will remain minimized, and no new Help Window will appear. The remedy is to manually restore the minimized Help Window.

2. **Names containing `a/l` or `a/p` are not supported.** In `add` and `edit`, a space followed by `a/` is treated as an address prefix, so names such as `Ravi a/l Kumar` cannot be entered as intended.

3. **Names in some scripts may not display correctly.** On some computers, e.g. macOS, names in scripts that join letters into combined shapes, such as Tamil (`கவி`) or Hindi (`प्रिया`), are shown as unrelated characters in the list, the detail panel and command results. Chinese, Japanese and Korean names are not affected. The name is still saved, searched and compared correctly; only how it is shown is affected.

These are the rules for each parameter. The command sections above give more details and examples.
Parameter | Prefix | Used in | Rules

`NAME` | `n/` | `add`, `edit` | Starts with a letter or digit. `PHONE` | `p/` | `add`, `edit` | 3 to 15 digits, optionally starting with `+`. Digit groups can be separated by single spaces or hyphens and enclosed in parentheses. Can end with `ext` and 1 to 6 digits, and a label in parentheses, e.g. `(65) 9123-4567 ext 12 (Office)`.
`EMAIL` | `e/` | `add`, `edit` | Of the form `local-part@domain`, e.g. `weiming@dbs.com`. See [`add`](#adding-a-supporter-add) for the full rules.
`ADDRESS` | `a/` | `add`, `edit` | Any text, not blank.
`ORGANISATION` | `o/` | `add`, `edit` | Any text, not blank, at most 100 characters.
`STAGE` | `st/` | `add`, `find`, `stage` | One of `prospect`, `contacted`, `cultivating`, `giving`, `lapsed` and `declined`, in upper or lower case.
`TAG` | `t/` | `add`, `edit`, `tag`, `untag` | English letters and digits only, with no spaces. Tags that differ only in capitalisation count as one tag.
`NOTE` | `nt/` | `log`, `editlog` | Any text, not blank, at most 500 characters.
`DATE` | `dt/` | `log`, `editlog` | A date in `yyyy-MM-dd` format, from `1900-01-01` to today.
`INTRODUCER_INDEX` | `by/` | `intro` | The index of the introducer in the displayed list. Leave it empty to remove the introducer.
`INDEX` | none | most commands | The supporter's number in the displayed list: a positive whole number such as `1`, `2` or `3`.
`ENTRY` | none | `editlog`, `unlog` | The interaction's number in the detail panel: a positive whole number.
`DAYS` | none | `quiet` | A whole number from `1` to `2147483647`.
`NAME_KEYWORD` | none | `find` | A word or part of a word in the supporter's name, e.g. `wei` for `Tan Wei Ming`.

In `edit`, `p/`, `e/`, `a/`, `o/` or `t/` with nothing after it clears that field instead (removing all tags for `t/`), as long as the supporter keeps a phone number or an email. In `add`, an empty prefix is rejected; leave the prefix out instead.

In `add` and `edit`, `t/` can be given more than once, and every other prefix only once. In `find`, every prefix can be given more than once, and the values of `o/`, `t/`, `p/` and `e/` are search text, matched as described in [`find`](#finding-supporters-by-name-or-other-fields-find).
